A1.justification: These are substantially revised versions of the same model-stitching study, retaining FuLA and several experimental settings. Both complete PDFs, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, figures and results sufficient for reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original stitching experiments involving adversarial training, shortcuts, class subsets and cross-layer alignment in Section 3 and Appendix B.

after.justification: V2 reports original standard and invariance-aware stitching experiments, input-validity checks and CKA comparisons in Section 3 and Appendices F–G.

M1.justification: V2 retains FuLA but introduces an invariance-aware procedure: generate identically represented inputs (IRIs), train the stitching transformation on these inputs, and evaluate on the corresponding non-inverted test data (Section 2.3.1). Applying this procedure to end-model-supervised objectives changes the method substantially beyond renaming or explaining FuLA.

E1.justification: CIFAR-10 and LS-ImageNet-10 remain, while v2 adds high-resolution ImageNet-100 and disjoint ImageNetB-100 classification and transfer settings. It also adds cross-bias tests involving models already trained on predictive pixel cues, unlike v1's previously unseen stitching-time shortcuts. V1's ArUco and location-only shortcut settings disappear.

E2.justification: The principal stitching comparators remain after matching TLM to HLM and the trained Hint objective to DM. However, v2 excludes HLM from the robust/non-robust comparisons (Figure 5 and Appendix F.4), where v1 included TLM. Appendix G also adds an invariance-aware CKA comparator alongside standard CKA.

E3.justification: V2 replaces accuracy-based similarity with normalized agreement probability and measures shortcut exploitation against permuted-cue controls. Initialization increases from 100 to 500 samples. The reported design replaces ResNet34 and residual-free ResNet18 with VGG16 and ViT configurations, drops mixed clean/adversarial stitching, and introduces distinct augmentation and batch-normalization policies for IRI training.

E4.justification: V1's class-subset, cross-layer, hint-depth and DM implementation analyses are removed. V2 adds IRI validity checks using identical models and paired original/inverted inputs (Appendix F.1), reports an augmentation control (Appendix B.2), and expands analysis of standard versus invariance-aware CKA (Appendix G). Shortcut and robustness analyses are substantially redesigned.

E5.justification: V1 identifies separate base-model instances but does not specify repeated-run averaging. V2 reports means across three random initializations, keeping the end model fixed and varying front models (Section 3; Appendix B.2). This is newly documented replication, not an established increase from a previously stated run count; uncertainty intervals and significance tests remain unspecified.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial result sets, including near-chance cross-bias similarity for IRI-trained DM, FuLA and SLM despite high standard-stitching similarity (Figure 2), and reduced unseen-cue exploitation (Figure 4). V1's baseline-accuracy table, class-subset results and cross-layer scores disappear. Changed metrics and training conditions prevent treating the new results as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 introduces the forward–backward compatibility requirement, formal relaxed/exact IRI sets, and a unique-optimal-forward-alignment assumption connecting IRI training to compatibility (Section 2.3.1). It also repairs FuLA's equation to match its stated downstream, penultimate-layer objective and defines normalized agreement in Appendix C. These substantially expand the formal framework, without adding theorem proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from FuLA as a more reliable stitching objective to invariance-aware stitching across multiple objectives. V2 explicitly includes FuLA among forward-only formulations that can mislead, claims backward compatibility mitigates these failures, and foregrounds robust/non-robust discrepancies and alignment-versus-shortcut tradeoffs.

C2.justification: V1 emphasizes task overfitting and FuLA's advantages; v2 explains misleading similarity through unmatched invariances and treats objective selection as an architecture-dependent tradeoff with no clear winner. It discusses relaxed-IRI semantic drift and SLM's failed ViT-Base identity check. The absence of a similarity oracle and restriction to image classification remain acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 supplies substantial new reproducibility information: IRI generation from uniform noise over 200 steps, resolution-specific parameters, SimCLR training, token-wise transformer stitching, hint selection, and augmentation/batch-statistics handling (Appendices A–D). It also adds a code-access URL. V1's cross-layer interpolation instructions disappear with that experiment.

R1.justification: Positioning moves from a knowledge-distillation-derived alignment objective toward shared invariances and bidirectional functional similarity. Previously cited Nanda and Jones work becomes foundational, while added references such as Feather, Goel and Klabunde support metamer, error-consistency and similarity-metric discussions. This changes the relationship to prior research substantially beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The introduction, methods organization, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten around forward–backward compatibility. Experiments are reordered, an integrated discussion is added, and appendices are reorganized from A–B into A–G. The title and TLM/HLM terminology also change.

P2.justification: V2 changes the main text to a two-column layout and substantially redesigns the visual presentation around standard-versus-IRI agreement plots. It replaces the opening conceptual illustration, removes cross-layer heatmaps and the baseline table, and adds sanity-check and expanded CKA panels. The retained FuLA schematic is updated and moved from v1 Figure 2 to v2 Appendix Figure 6.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is stronger validation of what functional similarity measures: v2 exposes cue-dependence failures of standard FuLA and tests an invariance-aware remedy with IRI/identity controls and broader architecture checks. Its qualified conclusions are better supported than v1's general preference for FuLA. Removing the baseline-accuracy table and cross-layer/class-subset analyses sacrifices useful evidence, and some identity checks still fail, but the stronger examination of the central claim provides a substantial net improvement.
